content: Hunter-gatherer communities are a window on how the human species learned to get a good night's rest. Here's what you can learn from them.When it comes to how our hunter-gatherer ancestors slept, there's a lot that we don't know. There's also some long-lasting assumptions, including the belief that they slept from dusk to dawn, that have recently been largely discredited.But research on today's foraging societies, often considered the best evidence we have for how we may have slept for more than 95% of human evolutionary history, has revealed a consistent finding: in general, people in foraging societies rarely report sleep problems."If you ask hunter-gatherers, 'Do you ever have trouble sleeping?' in their native language, they have trouble understanding the concept," says University of California, Los Angeles sleep scientist Jerome Siegel, who has studied the sleep patterns of Tanzania's Hadza, Bolivia's Tsimane and Namibia's San communities. That's even though the people who have been studied in non-industrial societies generally sleep less, and wake more, than those of us in industrialised ones.So what's their secret? Over the course of my reporting for my book The Sleep Myth and the BBC newsletter How to Sleep Better , I discovered some of the methods, approaches and ways of thinking that may have helped our ancient ancestors get their zzzs – and that the rest of us could incorporate to sleep a little bit better, too. Here are five of the most effective.Even if some aspects of our sleep quantity and quality are better, on average, in industrialised societies, one of the main foundations of sleep is not. And that's our circadian rhythms, the biological "clocks" that signal to our bodies when it's time to be awake and when to be sleepy – and which need consistent inputs from different cues called "zeitgebers" to stay on track.How to Sleep BetterFor more sleep insight and tips, you might like How to Sleep Better . Our free six-part email course features expert guidance for improving your sleep – and some of the tips may surprise you."We're living in environments that dysregulate this ancient timing system," says David Samson, director of the University of Toronto's Sleep and Human Evolution Lab and author of the book The Sleepless Ape: The Story of Sleep in Human Evolution.The primary zeitgeber – meaning "time giver" – is light, which is why researchers suggest that, as soon as you can after waking, you get any exposure that you can. Importantly, for those of us in industrialised societies, that doesn't just help keep our circadian rhythms on track. It may also blunt the effect of using artificial light at night (which, for what it's worth, might also not be quite as bad for us as we thought).Researchers have found that while using a very bright screen for several hours before bedtime might delay sleep onset by about 10 minutes , that effect disappeared if participants also experienced bright light exposure during the day .Of course, this can be hard in darker climes, or for those of us who work indoors. But small spells might help, so the next time you have the option to walk a few extra minutes instead of take the train, eat lunch outside instead of indoors, or work at a desk under a window, take it.Another environmental input that could help with our sleep? Temperature – which, even in hot climates, tends to fall over the course of the night and rise again during the day.Scientists like Siegel think it may be an especially underrated one, pointing to how non-industrial groups like the Hadza tend to go to sleep a few hours after sunset and wake before sunrise, with their timings tracking temperature, not light.In industrialised societies, many of us live in homes where the temperature stays the same, day and night. To get some of the effect, he says, try turning the thermostat down a few degrees before bed, setting a smart thermostat to fall over the course of the night, or opening a window.And yes: both light and temperature change over the course of the year – and the sleep of hunter-gatherers changes with them . That's not just in terms of timings, but also sleep durations, with people sleeping less when days are longer and warmer, and more when they're shorter and colder.So, while many people in these societies tend to wake up around the same time each day (and that's another way that we can help re-entrain our circadian rhythms), not worrying about our sleep shifting with the seasons is important, too.When evening sets in in foraging societies, people don't immediately go to bed, researchers told me. They engage in relaxing, non-work-centred activities – whether gathering around campfires, telling stories, or visiting each other."The moment the Sun goes down, everything starts getting quiet," says anthropologist Alyssa Crittenden at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, who has spent time with Tanzania's Hadza each year for two decades. "During the day, most activity and conversations revolve around really practical matters. They revolve around logistics, they revolve around childcare, they revolve around food… But at night, you're done with that."The fact that the evening is "radically different" from the more work-oriented daylight hours is "extremely important," she adds – and one more signal to our bodies, and brains, that it's time for sleep. It's yet another reason, for those who are able, to kick the habit of checking work emails or paying bills right before bed – and for leaders in the workplace to stop expecting employees to do so, too.For the past few months, nurse Dale Weiser has been making unexpected home visits.As the state battles the deadliest measles outbreak in recent history, the clinical supervisor drives 30 miles (48.3km), sometimes daily, to a rural corner of Pennsylvania where many Amish people live.Walking into strangers' homes, Weiser says she tries her best to be respectful and non-intrusive as she vaccinates dozens of family members against the measles, sometimes around the kitchen table."A lot of people that I encounter, they don't have health insurance. They don't have a lot of interaction with the health system, and they just haven't seen the need to get these vaccines," said Weiser, who works for the Chester County Health Department."When you start talking and you answer their questions, and build that trust, a lot of times they will make a different decision."The at-home vaccinations are part of the county and state health departments' strategy to encourage immunisations in the county, which includes an Amish community who abstain from many aspects of modern life, including regular contact with the western medical system.The state health department told the BBC it has administered nearly 4,300 measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines at pop-up clinics near the epicentre of the outbreak since it began in late April.But even as health officials see success in their vaccine programmes, the state has reported four deaths from measles complications, marking the most deadly outbreak the US has seen since 1992.The infections have led to tensions between state and federal health officials, including vaccine-sceptic Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.Those politics are back of mind in the Amish community, where people are growing fearful of more deaths as they watch their friends and family fall sick with the disease, which for decades has been eliminated in the US."They're not a community that's as easy to reach - we can't just put up a social media post," Weiser said. "They are suffering at the moment, and we're trying to reach out and make connections."Amish people began coming to the US in the early 1700s, with the first community settling in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Known as the "Plain People" for the simple clothes they wear, the Amish are a devout Christian community that does not use many forms of technology, relying on horse and buggies instead of cars.About 90,000 Amish people live in Pennsylvania, with estimates suggesting around only a quarter of Amish people in the Lancaster area have had the MMR vaccine.There is no particular religious text advising against vaccines, but Amish people do not have regular contact with the western medical system, or have a way to easily travel to appointments, experts said."A lot of people who haven't gotten vaccinated, it's not because they have a strong stance against getting vaccinated for measles. It's just that they haven't gotten around to it. It's not convenient," said Braxton Mitchell, a genetic epidemiologist with University of Maryland School of Medicine who runs a research clinic studying the Amish in Lancaster.Amish people are extremely social, he said, so when the virus hits one church group, it affects everyone who is unvaccinated."Measles is rampant in the Amish community," he said. "People are concerned about it."He added the community has been especially concerned about the dangers to babies; so far two newborns have died of measles complications, as well as an 18-year-old and a 40-year-old woman, according to state officials.Chester County public health officials did not wait long to launch a response to the growing measles outbreak in their community, which shares a border with Lancaster County, the epicentre of the outbreak.Jeanne Franklin, the director of the health department, said officials have been using some of the strategies they employed during the Covid pandemic - knocking on doors in the community to let them know about the outbreak and offering private settings, like people's homes, for immunisations.

WHO expands safe options for contraception
From emergency contraception to longer-lasting implants and future contraceptives for men, the World Health Organization (WHO) is recommending a wider range of safe and effective options so people can choose contraception that meets their needs.
An estimated 164 million women who want to delay or avoid pregnancy are not using contraception, underscoring the urgent need for better and expanded access to contraceptives.
With the new publication, “WHO guidelines on expanding contraceptive options” , WHO aims to help countries broaden access to methods supported by the best available evidence.
This can help ensure that people have a wider range of options so they can make informed decisions about whether to use contraception, which method is right for them, and when to change or stop it.
The new guidelines offer people alternative ways of using existing methods. To this end, WHO recommends that combined oral contraceptive pills can be taken for extended periods of up to six months or continuously for up to one year, as alternatives to cyclical use. WHO supports use of contraceptive implants for up to five years, potentially reducing the need for replacement procedures, clinic visits and associated costs.
WHO recommends mifepristone as an additional emergency contraception option, taken as soon as possible and within five days of unprotected sex. The evidence shows that mifepristone at doses of 10 – 50 mg is likely to be as safe and effective as other emergency contraceptive methods.
“Choice is a gender equality issue,” said Pascale Allotey, Director of WHO’s Department of Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Child and Adolescent Health and Ageing. “Contraception isn't one-size-fits-all. Men and women both need a range of options that reflect what science and innovation can now offer, weighed against convenience, invasiveness, behaviour, reliability and accessibility. Real choice means the confidence and control to choose a method, change it, or stop it.”
Expanding access also means being clear about which methods are not yet supported by sufficient evidence. In this regard, WHO has called for more research around ormeloxifene before inclusion in family planning programs because the current evidence on safety is limited. The new guideline further recommends against adding quinestrol-containing contraceptive pills to national contraceptive programmes due to limited evidence and reports of serious adverse events.
While the new guideline expands the evidence base for existing contraceptive methods, WHO is also working to broaden the range of contraceptive choices available in the future. Today, men have relatively few methods under their control – principally condoms, withdrawal and vasectomy. Yet even with those limited choices, around 30% of couples rely on a male method.
WHO research challenges a longstanding assumption that men would not use new contraceptives. More than 75% of couples surveyed said they would be willing to use a new male contraceptive, while more than 85% of women said they would trust their male partners to take responsibility for contraception.
To help turn that demand into new products, WHO has developed its first Target Product Profile for male contraceptive methods, setting out the characteristics future methods should aim to meet, including safety, effectiveness, acceptability and affordability. The aim is to give researchers, funders and developers clearer direction and help shape a market that better reflects what people want and need.
Several hormonal and non-hormonal male methods are being researched, and several promising candidates are in advanced clinical trials, suggesting that new reversible male contraceptives may be in the market within the next 5-10 years.
WHO aims to support countries in updating their policies and plans to support family planning backed by the best available science.
Note to editors
The global study on male contraception cited above, “Socio-behavioral factors linked to willingness to use new male contraceptives: a cross-sectional survey of men and female partners across four low- and middle-income countries,” was published in the journal Contraception.
Dedicated to the well-being of all people and guided by science, WHO leads and champions global efforts to give everyone, everywhere, an equal chance at a safe and healthy life. We are the United Nations’ agency for health that connects nations, partners and people in more than 150 locations – leading the world’s response to health emergencies, preventing disease, addressing the root causes of health issues and expanding access to medicines and health care.
Our mission is to support all countries to promote, provide and protect health. “Together for health. Stand with science”, the theme of World Health Day 2026, marks a year-long campaign to highlight science as the foundation for protecting health and well-being worldwide.
